title: Hymns of the mind
hook: the mind is called restless, and the Word is its rest

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pilgrimages: the Guru among the pilgrims, and against a tax to come near God. Your line was free pilgrims. Did you question the charge, or quietly cover one? Day one thousand one hundred ninety.

It's the middle of the night, and a mind is trying to solve itself. It runs the plan again, the conversation again, the worst case again. Each time it gets a little cleverer, and a little less rested. Guru Amar Das, in the Anand, his song of bliss, turns to exactly that mind and speaks to it: e man chanchala, O restless mind. Not to scold it. To tell it something it keeps missing about cleverness. Across this week we've heard him talk to the mind more than once. Today we listen to what he tells it about rest.
screen: `A MIND TRYING TO SOLVE ITSELF.` → `E MAN CHANCHALA.` → `WHAT CLEVERNESS MISSES.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, paraphrased: O restless mind, no one has found Him through cleverness. Listen, my mind, no one has found Him through cleverness. This enticing Maya has led people astray in doubt. And the verse ends where it began: O restless mind, no one has found Him through cleverness. Chanchal means restless, flickering, never still. And the mind's favorite tool for getting still is cleverness: one more plan, one more argument, one more way of being sure. The Guru says that tool doesn't reach the place the mind is trying to get to. Notice he repeats the line. The warning comes back, and the verse closes on it, the way you'd say something twice to someone who's tired and not quite hearing you. So where is rest? The Anand's opening verse points the way, again paraphrased: I have found the True Guru, with ease, and my mind rings with rejoicing; sing the Word, all of you who have let it dwell in the mind. Rest, in that picture, comes through the Word. Not a new idea to win with, but the Guru's Word, heard, sung, remembered, until the mind stops having to hold itself up. So the Anand says to the restless mind: you can't think your way into rest, but you can rest in the Word. That's the line for the week's end.
screen: `E MAN CHANCHALA: O RESTLESS MIND.` · `NOT FOUND THROUGH CLEVERNESS.` · `SAID AGAIN, FOR A TIRED LISTENER.` · `SING THE WORD, AT EASE.` · then, large: `REST IN THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest your mind in one line. Choose one line from this week to rest in. Man too jot saroop hai. Or by any door. Or simply Waheguru. Settle, and breathe. Let the line ride on the breath, in and out. When the mind starts solving, planning or arguing, don't fight it with more cleverness. Just notice, and lay it back down on the line, the way you'd lay a tired child back on a pillow. The line holds the mind. The bell holds the time.
Hymns of the mind. Guru Amar Das calls the mind restless, says cleverness never finds the Lord, and offers the Word as its rest. Today's word.
Your line: rest in the word. Tonight, if the mind starts running the plan again, say your one line slowly, and let it do the holding. Day one thousand one hundred ninety.

howItsDone: The Anand Sahib, with its verses to the restless mind, is part of the Sikh daily banis, and its opening and closing pauris are sung at the end of gatherings at the gurdwara.

notes: Editor pass: removed a wrong paraphrase of pauri 10's close (it speaks of Maya made by the One who made attachment sweet, not of the Word filling the mind with sweetness); the verse now ends on its own refrain, and rest through the Word is drawn from Anand pauri 1 (added to sources). Hook no longer opens on a Punjabi line like day 1183's; the week recap was cut so it does not duplicate day 1191's close.

The Anand verse to the restless mind is cited as pauri 10, Ang 918, and paraphrased from memory, including the closing turn (the One who made the enticement gives the Word, and the mind is filled with sweetness). Please check the pauri number, Ang and paraphrase.
